title: ThunderSyncRL: Lossless Accelerationof Agentic Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: ThunderSyncRL: Lossless Acceleration of Agentic Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract: Abstract Language models are moving beyond generating answers to pursuing long-horizon goals in interactive environments. Post-training these agents requires long, heterogeneous trajectories, and synchronous systems leave learner engines idle until rollout and verification finish. To squeeze out these pipeline bubbles, asynchronous training overlaps rollout and learning across updates, but comes at the cost of policy staleness. We introduce ThunderSyncRL , which starts gradient computation as soon as all required inputs are fixed, without policy staleness. For group relative policy optimization (GRPO), ThunderSyncRL computes each trajectory’s score gradient as soon as the reward for that trajectory arrives, without waiting for the group. For on-policy distillation (OPD), it computes gradients for each completed agentic turn’s teacher-scored actions while tool calls run in the sandbox. We prove that gradient streaming produces the same GRPO and OPD updates as batch-synchronous training, without changing either objective. On SWE-bench Verified and Terminal Bench 4.0, we train models to the same performance up to 1.9 × 1.9\times faster than synchronous training. With zero policy staleness, ThunderSyncRL also outperforms asynchronous training at a fixed budget by up to 2.47 2.47 percentage points.

Figure 1: ThunderSyncRL matches Sync’s SWE-bench Verified pass@3 at up to 1.9 × 1.9\times lower training cost under GRPO (left pair) and OPD (right pair). At a 128-GPU-hour budget, its zero-staleness schedule improves pass@3 by up to 2.47 percentage points over Async and Fully Async, both of which admit stale rollouts. 1 Introduction Language models are increasingly trained as agents for long-horizon decision-making in interactive environments, reasoning and using tools in response to feedback. Reinforcement learning (RL) from environment or verifier feedback has emerged as a promising way to improve this behavior [ 22 , 10 , 28 , 45 , 13 ] . However, training these agents requires interaction trajectories that are expensive to generate and heterogeneous in duration, with long-tailed completion times [ 19 , 4 , 36 ] . In batch-synchronous RL, learner engines remain idle until rollout engines finish the batch and all rewards arrive [ 11 , 36 ] . We found that learner GPUs sit idle for 49.5% of step time in synchronous GRPO and OPD training while they wait for rollout and verification (Figure 3 ). Prior work reports idle fractions as high as 81% [ 36 ] , and the slowest 10% of rollout requests can take up to half of rollout time [ 33 ] , which itself accounts for 70% to over 90% of training time [ 12 , 57 ] . Existing systems reduce these pipeline bubbles, idle gaps between dependent stages, by overlapping computation and coordinating resource allocation [ 26 , 39 , 55 , 11 , 16 ] . Asynchronous execution overlaps rollout and learning across updates, but some trajectories come from older policies. This policy staleness can require extra algorithmic machinery, including importance-weighted off-policy correction, filtering, clipping, or explicit staleness control [ 9 , 11 , 16 , 17 ] . On-policy pipelines overlap execution within a fixed rollout, but complete-group schedules still delay trajectory-local backward passes until all group rewards arrive [ 7 ] . We argue that the apparent trade-off between pipeline overlap and zero staleness is artifactual, arising from coarse execution barriers. Although a synchronous update requires the complete batch, its gradient computation can begin earlier. For example, in group relative policy optimization (GRPO) [ 37 ] , group rewards determine how to weight each trajectory’s score gradient, but the gradient can be computed before all rewards arrive. We therefore ask: can learner computation begin as soon as its objective dependencies are satisfied with zero staleness? We introduce ThunderSyncRL , which streams gradients through dependency-aware scheduling of learner work. During update k k , trajectories are sampled from π θ k \pi_{\theta_{k}} and gradients are evaluated at θ k \theta_{k} . For GRPO, a trajectory’s advantage seems to need every reward in its group. ThunderSyncRL nevertheless starts that trajectory’s backward pass as soon as its own reward arrives, and two running sums of score gradients recover the exact group gradient once the group closes (Section 3.4 ). For on-policy distillation (OPD) [ 1 ] , ThunderSyncRL releases a turn’s student backward pass once a frozen teacher scores the turn’s action tokens, allowing overlap with tool execution and later turns. After all trajectories, groups, and gradient work finish, ThunderSyncRL combines the gradients, takes one optimizer step, and publishes θ k + 1 \theta_{k+1} . ThunderSyncRL is therefore asynchronous in execution and synchronous in policy updates. We use SWE-smith and SETA-Env for post-training [ 49 , 38 ] and evaluate on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal Bench 4.0 [ 21 , 27 ] . Our scheduling analysis predicts step wall time speedup approaching 2 × 2\times over synchronous execution when rollout and learner work are balanced and the residual tail and publication cost vanish. With a fixed trajectory batch size, shorter steps let ThunderSyncRL learn from more trajectories within the same GPU-hours, potentially improving end-to-end performance. Figure 1 compares ThunderSyncRL with Sync by training cost: each arrow marks where ThunderSyncRL reaches the pass@3 of a Sync checkpoint, at 1.6 1.6 to 1.9 × 1.9\times lower cost. Our main contributions are as follows: • We introduce ThunderSyncRL and gradient streaming, overlapping rollout and learner computation while preserving a synchronous optimizer step and zero policy staleness. • We derive exact gradient reductions for GRPO and turn-level OPD, allowing early backward computation while preserving their batch-synchronous updates. • We evaluate ThunderSyncRL on SWE-bench Verified and Terminal Bench 4.0 under GRPO and OPD. ThunderSyncRL reaches the common pass@3 targets up to 1.9× faster than Sync while retaining zero policy staleness. At 128 GPU-hours, ThunderSyncRL achieves the highest pass@3 in all settings, 1.27 to 2.47 points above Async. 2 Related Work Figure 2: Schematic schedules for GRPO (a) and OPD (b). ∙ \bullet Sync waits for full batches; ∙ \bullet Async overlaps adjacent batches with one-step staleness; ∙ \bullet Fully Async updates rollout weights while trajectories remain in flight. ∙ \bullet ThunderSyncRL streams ready gradients with one batch-synchronous optimizer step and zero staleness. 2.1 Post-training with Reinforcement Learning Towards Agentic Tasks RL post-training extends single-turn generation to agents that learn through long-horizon interaction with external environments. ArCHer develops hierarchical multi-turn RL, while DigiRL combines offline and online RL for mobile-device control [ 56 , 2 ] . Web and search agents learn through self-evolving curricula, browser interaction, and outcome rewards [ 31 , 46 , 22 , 40 , 6 , 53 ] . Tool-use research studies strategic interpreter use, fine-grained rewards, planning supervision, and dynamic user interaction [ 10 , 32 , 24 , 52 ] . Further work addresses trajectory-level optimization failures, multi-step supervision, and procedural or capability-targeted training environments [ 44 , 15 , 8 , 41 , 23 ] . Software agents learn from executable environments, software-evolution data, and execution feedback [ 28 , 45 , 13 ] . Agent Lightning and VerlTool provide reusable infrastructure across heterogeneous agent workflows [ 25 , 20 ] . 2.2 Optimization of Reinforcement Learning Distributed RLHF systems coordinate generation, reference and reward inference, and actor and critic training, using model placement, device reallocation, and stage fusion to reduce idle time [ 50 , 18 , 26 , 39 , 55 ] . Building on actor-learner decoupling in distributed RL [ 9 , 29 ] , LlamaRL, AReaL, AsyncFlow, and StreamRL support disaggregated generation and training, streaming execution, asynchronous weight synchronization, and control of policy staleness [ 47 , 11 , 16 , 54 ] . For heterogeneous agentic rollouts, PipelineRL and RolloutPipe pipeline rollout and learner execution [ 30 , 7 ] . JigsawRL, Libra, TideRL, and WAR address fine-grained scheduling, elastic resource allocation, long tails, and inference caching [ 19 , 4 , 36 , 48 ] . SAO performs asynchronous optimization from individually completed rollouts [ 17 ] . ThunderSyncRL schedules learner computation as each objective source becomes ready, overlapping it with unfinished rollouts while preserving a fixed policy snapshot and a single synchronous optimizer step. The agent, reward, and optimization objective remain unchanged. 3 Methods We present ThunderSyncRL, a gradient streaming framework for zero-stale agentic post-training (Figure 2 ). ThunderSyncRL releases learner computation when each source becomes ready . Exact gradient reduction and a synchronous optimizer barrier preserve the update semantics of GRPO and on-policy distillation (OPD) while allowing rollout and learning to overlap. 3.1 Background Group relative policy optimization (GRPO). Given a prompt, GRPO samples a group of trajectories and normalizes their rewards within the group to obtain relative advantages. The policy update weights each trajectory’s scored action-token log probabilities by its detached advantage. On-policy distillation (OPD). OPD generates trajectories with the student policy and evaluates the student’s action tokens under a frozen teacher. The resulting token-level supervision defines a distillation loss for the action tokens of each agentic turn. Figure 3: Pipeline bubbles in synchronous agentic RL. GPU utilization during GRPO training on SWE-smith, with four rollout GPUs above the axis and four learner GPUs below. Rollout utilization (busy share of generation slots) drops as long-tail trajectories finish. Hatched bands mark idle time. ∙ \bullet Sync learners wait for the last reward for 49.5% of each step, and rollout GPUs wait while the learner trains. ∙ \bullet ThunderSyncRL starts each trajectory’s backward pass when its reward arrives and completes 15 optimizer steps in the GPU-hours Sync needs for 8. Actor-learner execution protocols. Agentic reinforcement learning alternates between two expensive stages: generating long, tool-using trajectories and optimizing the policy from the resulting training signals. Conventional synchronous training places a batch barrier between these stages, leaving the learner idle until every trajectory and reward is available (Figure 3 ). Fully asynchronous methods remove this idle time, but typically update the policy while older rollouts remain in flight, introducing policy staleness. ThunderSyncRL follows a single principle: each computation is released at the earliest time when its mathematical dependencies are satisfied. 3.2 Problem Formulation Objective sources. Consider update k k with policy π 𝜽 k \pi_{{\bm{\theta}}_{k}} and logical rollout batch ℬ k \mathcal{B}_{k} . Each trajectory is a sequence of agentic turns, where a turn contains a policy-generated action and the resulting environment or tool observation.
